en: Until I return again,
Until your eyes see me again,
Remain safe, my cave.
I am leaving with no way out.
Forgive the duty I owe you,
My dear, dear cave!
My ditch that channels the water,
Until I return again,
Remain safe, Bakay, my elder!
I hid myself away from Talas.
Because I had grown exhausted,
Because no kinsman would stand up for me,
I took Semetey away in flight.
Gray-maned khan, if you do not watch over me,
Will I, poor wretch, collapse exhausted?
O God, my six tail-feathers, forty flight-feathers—
Will they be broken?
From my hero himself,
The orphan I received as a gift—
O God, shall I lose him?
I hid myself along Keng-Kol.
Because of the humiliation I suffered,
Because of the six villains,
The little one I received as a gift,
I took away and fled.
Who followed twelve spiritual masters,
To whom ten saints opened the way,
Whose protector Khojosan
Strove at his side,
To whom Ak Eshen pledged his hand,
Standing ready close beside him—
My leopard prince, be my helper!
I stand here unable to find support.
Forty Chiltens who protected my Bloodstained One,
Be helpers to my only child!
I have set out; God, protect me!
My tiger Manas, my leopard,
Protect my orphan!
Among horses, the white-headed winged steed;
Almambet and Chubak, names that chime together,
Martyrs, I go battered and disheveled!
Hear my words;
If anything is crooked, set it straight;
Protect my orphan.
My wings have been caught in fire;
I am leaving, unable to turn back.
Where God has dug a pit,
Through that place I go;
Along a sheer cliff no goose can circle,
O God, along its flank I go.
My Serek and my Syrgak,
Protect me, my two lights!”
Her voice was heard by God.
Your wretched mother Kanykey
Entered the mausoleum and fell.
The mausoleum's interior resounded;
Oh, mercy, a murmuring voice spoke.
When your sister-in-law was humiliated,
Abyke had brought her trouble.
There appeared directly before her,
Before your fierce, heroic sister-in-law,
A white-bearded dervish.
“Hey, Kanykey, my little foal,
Regret cannot remedy what has passed;
Grief for the departed brings no benefit!
There is no fleet steed to catch and ride.
Do not grieve, Kanykey;
You have no kinsman other than courage.
You have no ridge where you can shelter.
Do not grieve so bitterly, unfortunate one;
You have no kinsman other than courage!
Do not sob, Kanykey;
What will sobbing accomplish?
Rise and take courage.
With your mother and Semetey,
You shall reach your destination, poor soul.”
Startled, she woke from sleep.
Her agitated heart grew calm;
Your sister-in-law opened her eyes.
There was not even a bird, much less a person.
It was a day for falling into torment.
Your father's grave, this world is shit!
“Was my plea to Allah a cry of grief?
Between sleep and waking,
The old man who was speaking—
Perhaps he was my father Kyzyr.
God may grant my wish,
To make this visit of devotion,
Then to reach Bukhara.
My river whose expanse is like a lake,
If I see her, my heart will be at peace.
I have no companion besides my mother.
God may grant my wish;
Carrying my orphan son,
Perhaps my poor mother is coming.
It will not go well if I enter this open ground.
From this yellow plain, open as the moon,
If the villains attack, it will not go well.
Tracking my every footprint,
Will the six villains pursue me relentlessly?
Tormenting me, tracking every footprint,
Will they chase me till I turn pale?
Will God strike me down like this?”
“I put my trust in God!” she cried;
Your sister-in-law walked without stopping.
Her tears fell like hail;
Water streamed from her nose like a spring.
The wide world had grown narrow.
Your sister-in-law, who would not eat even tail-fat,
Now longed even for wild thistles.
Your bereft sister-in-law Kanykey,
With so many wounds upon her,
Your sister-in-law grieved and cried.
Your sister-in-law went on foot
Through the hollow of Uyurmo-Kyr,
Skirting its edge without rest.
How could your sister-in-law spare herself?
At three places she wept and cried aloud.
When your sister-in-law sighed,
Flames billowed from her mouth.
She walked shrieking, nursing her pain.
Your sister-in-law Kanykey cried aloud,
Leaning on Syr Barang,
Supporting herself along Uch-Koshoy.
The whole of her body
Was drenched in pitch-black blood.
She grew faint, her limbs dangling.
To a saddle-shaped mountain pass,
She had barely managed to reach.
Without strength to walk,
Her child and her mother,
The poor widow could not see.
Her eyes dimmed, her heart seethed;
Her strength failed, her misery seethed.
Your sister-in-law stood exhausted.
That dear mother Chyyyrdy,
An elder who had reached eighty,
Had taken the cradle-child
And pressed him to her breast.
Your saintly mother Chyyyrdy,
When she saw Kanykey's face,
Showing her advanced years,
For the fierce woman who had suffered hell,
Made the infant Semetey
Laugh and beam just then.
Gathering courage, the elder,
Dear Chyyyrdy, the blessed saint, said:
“Oh, Kanykey, my little foal,
Do not keep sobbing and weeping.
My child, do not keep wailing and crying.
Now that your hero, your prince, has died,
Gird your waist, Kanykey.
What can we do by staying here?
When a khan dies, his wife
Finds her own kin close to her.
Let us go toward Karakan;
Let us pour out the sorrow within us.
Come, my child, let us flee toward Karakan.
Oh, Kanykey, my little foal,
Sitting here in grief and lament,
What wish shall we fulfill?
To the city of your father Temir Khan,
Let us wander in!
Oh, Kanykey, my little foal,
Brittle iron is not tempered steel;
Dogs reared elsewhere are no people of ours.
Scraps of iron joined together are not tempered steel;
Dogs reared as slaves from the beginning are no people of ours.
This Talas is no homeland for us.
A little falcon will not be our hunting hawk;
Wandering dogs will not become our people.
We reared a kite; it will not become a hunting hawk.
Dogs reared as slaves will not become our people.
Gird your waist and take courage;
My heroic child, rise!
Before the fate decreed by the Creator,
My child Kanykey, take courage.
What you see today is gone tomorrow.
My child Kanykey, such is this shitty world!
Among horses, even the bay winged steed has passed away.
From this very world,
Alexander and the lion Chinggis have passed away.
This faithless thing whose bottom has fallen out—
Who has ever had their fill of this false world?
Our father Adam has passed away too.
And more than that, Kanykey,
My little foal, even the lion, His Holiness Ali, has passed away.
My banner fastened to the spear,
My orphan here before us,
Is your gift left by Magnanimous Manas.
Your hoof left by the winged steed,
This Semetey here,
Is your little one left by your white hawk Manas.
Your spring flowing from the foothills,
Your little one left by the Magnanimous One,
Your bright star in heaven,
Your ruby and otter fur at your collar,
Your soft little mottled gray hawk,
This Semetey here
Is your gray goshawk, your morning star.
The one I open my mouth to kiss,
The one I open my eyes to see,
My spring flowing through the valley,
My little one borne at death's door,
My inheritance left by Manas,
The shelter over my head,
Infant Semetey
Is the luck upon my brow.
Let them not come over along the foothills;
Let them not fall upon us from above.
Let them not seize the orphan
And do whatever they please.
Digging your pit deep,
Let them not make your misery seethe, my child Kanykey.”
The two ladies led one another along,
Coughing as they followed the road.
The orphan still of cradle age,
They carried with his little limbs waving.
The two ladies carried him by turns.
Unable to cross the ridge on foot,
When they saw shrubs, bushes, or stones,
The two ladies tried to hide, but could not fit beneath them.
(False world, may you come to ruin!)
Nor could they lie down on open ground.
Unable to cross Chapchak Pass,
The two ladies were exhausted, weeping, unable to walk.
Without overshoes, wearing only felt socks,
If death does not come for its due, the wretched soul must suffer.
Without boots, wearing only felt socks,
The poor little soul would not die.
When she tried to walk, her strength failed.
Black blood flowed from her calves;
The ends of her bones throbbed;
The soles of her feet were torn to pieces.
The six villains had plundered the court.
He was still a cradle-child;
For six whole days Semetey
Had tasted no food.
Unable to raise a loud cry,
Nor could her child recover his senses.
That dear sister-in-law of yours, Kanykey, said:
“If the child is lost to hunger,
What shall I do by going to Bukhara?
Rather than that, for my orphan,
O God, let me be sacrificed!
Dark night! Perhaps all hope will leave us today;
Perhaps his appointed death will come today.
Ah, my dear mother,
Perhaps the child will die of hunger.
For the infant, my only one,
Perhaps death will come today.
For me, this bereaved, unhappy woman,
Perhaps all hope will leave today!”
When she offered her breast, there was no milk.
Dark night descended upon her.
Your mother Chyyyrdy had no strength;
